title: Average
summary: One guaranteed question in almost every Tier 1 shift: a member joining or leaving, a batsman's innings, or a weighted two-group average. The whole topic collapses to one habit — convert averages to sums (Sum = Avg × n) before touching anything.

subtopics.title: Average & the sum bridge
subtopics.concept:
$\text{Average} = \dfrac{\text{Sum of observations}}{\text{Number of observations}}$. The useful direction is the reverse: **Sum = Average × n** — most CGL average questions are solved by converting to sums immediately.

**Properties:**
- If every observation is increased by k, the average increases by k (same for −, ×, ÷).
- The average is always between the smallest and largest observation.
- If all numbers are equal, average = each number; the sum of deviations from the average is zero.

**Standard averages** (memorise): first n naturals $= \frac{n+1}{2}$; first n odd $= n$; first n even $= n+1$; squares $= \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$; cubes $= \frac{(n+1)^2}{4}$.
**Consecutive numbers:** average = middle term = $\frac{\text{first} + \text{last}}{2}$.

tricks.title: Sum = average × n first
tricks.body: Never manipulate averages directly — flip to sums, adjust, divide back.

example.q: The average of 8 numbers is 32.5. Find their sum.

tricks.title: Uniform shift
tricks.body: Adding k to every number just adds k to the average.

example.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. If each number is multiplied by 3 and increased by 5, find the new average.

tricks.title: Middle of consecutive terms
tricks.body: For evenly spaced numbers, the average is the central value — no addition needed.

example.q: The average of 5 consecutive numbers is 30. Find the largest.

mistakes: Reporting a sum where an average is asked (read the units).
Averaging two averages with different group sizes (a 40-60 'average of averages' error).
Using $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$-style sums without dividing by n when the average is asked.
For 'each multiplied by 3 and increased by 5', applying only one of the two operations.

subtopics.title: Members joining or leaving
subtopics.concept:
When a new member joins (or one leaves) and the average changes, the key quantity is the **total sum**, not the average.

- New member whose entry changes the average from $A$ to $A'$ (group of n): value $= A' + n(A' - A)$.
- Member leaving: removed value $= A' + n(A - A')$, where A' is the new average of the remaining n.
- Replacement of one member: new − old $= n(A' - A)$, i.e. replaced value $= \text{old} + n(\text{change})$.

Equivalent view: the new member must carry the extra $n(A' - A)$ for all the old members **plus** his own share $A'$.

tricks.title: Joining: own share + extras
tricks.body: New value = new average + (number of old members) × (average jump).

example.q: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. When their teacher joins, the average becomes 15. Find the teacher's age.

tricks.title: Replacement: n × jump added
tricks.body: Only the swapped item changes the sum, by exactly n × (average change).

example.q: The average of 8 numbers is 24. If 20 is replaced by 44, the new average is:

tricks.title: Exclusion: subtract the sums
tricks.body: Old total − (new count × new average) = removed value.

example.q: The average of 9 numbers is 27. If one number is excluded the average becomes 25. Find the excluded number.

mistakes: Using the OLD average where the NEW one is needed in the member formula.
Counting the new member inside n (n refers to the members BEFORE the change in the joining formula).
For replacement, computing the new number as old + change (missing the factor n).
Sign errors when the average falls instead of rising.

subtopics.title: Weighted average & two-group problems
subtopics.concept:
When groups of different sizes are combined, the combined average is the **weighted** mean:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2 + n_3 \bar{x}_3}{n_1 + n_2 + n_3}$$

It always lies closer to the bigger group's average. Alligation (cross method) works too — see the Mixture topic.

**Two unknown averages:** if a group's average is missing, compute total sums group-wise and divide. Keep every product written down; these questions are pure bookkeeping.

tricks.title: Totals, not averages
tricks.body: Convert each group to a total, add, divide by the combined count.

example.q: In a class of 60 students, 20 girls have an average of 40 marks. If the class average is 50, find the boys' average.

tricks.title: Balance point intuition
tricks.body: The combined average divides the gap between the two group averages in the ratio n₂ : n₁ (inverse of sizes).

example.q: 20 boys average 12 years, 30 girls average 11 years. Combined average?
example.solution: $\frac{240 + 330}{50} = 11.4$ years — four parts from 11, one from 12, as 30 : 20 predicts.

tricks.title: Newcomer pushing a known average
tricks.body: Combined-average questions with a single newcomer reduce to value = A' + n(A' − A).

example.q: 15 workers average ₹250 in wages. A manager joins and the average becomes ₹300. Find the manager's wage.

mistakes: Combining averages directly (30 and 40 do not average to 35 unless the groups are equal).
Dividing by the wrong combined count (students + teacher, workers + manager).
Weighing with the wrong side of the alligation cross.
Rounding intermediate sums — these questions usually come out exact; a decimal mid-way means a slip.

subtopics.title: Batsman problems, overlapping sums & multi-step sets
subtopics.concept:
**Batsman/cricketer template:** a score in the next innings raises the average by d. If the new average is A' after n innings, the score was $A' + (n-1)d$. Rearranged: new average $= \frac{\text{old total} + \text{score}}{n}$.

**Overlapping sums** (temperatures, marks): if the average of Mon–Wed is a and of Tue–Thu is b, subtracting gives Thu − Mon = 3(b − a). Give one endpoint to find the other.

**Split sets:** an average over n numbers with partial averages over overlapping or consecutive chunks is solved by converting every average to a sum and using one variable for the unknown chunk.

tricks.title: Batsman: work in totals
tricks.body: Old total + new score = new count × new average.

example.q: A batsman scores 87 in his 17th innings and thereby increases his average by 3. Find his average after the 17th innings.

tricks.title: Overlap: subtract the sums
tricks.body: The shared days cancel, leaving the difference of the end days.

example.q: The average temperature of Mon, Tue, Wed is 37°C and of Tue, Wed, Thu is 34°C. If Monday was 40°C, find Thursday.

tricks.title: One variable for the unknown chunk
tricks.body: Name the smallest unknown x, express the rest from the given relations, and let the leftover sum close the equation.

example.q: 8 numbers average 20. First two average 15.5, next three average 21⅓. The 6th is 5 less than the 7th, and the 8th is 7 more than the 7th. Find the 8th.

mistakes: In batsman problems, multiplying by n instead of (n − 1) for the old total.
Subtracting the averages (37 − 34) and reporting 3 as Thu − Mon without multiplying by the overlap length rule.
Forgetting that the 'next' chunk overlaps the previous one (11 numbers: first 6 and last 6 share the 6th).
Setting the relations backwards (6th is 5 LESS than 7th ⇒ 7th = 6th + 5).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Average age/weight/marks of a group; a teacher, manager or new member joins (or someone leaves); new average given.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert to totals. Newcomer = A' + n(A' − A); leaver = A' + n(A − A'). Check with total sums.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A number/weight is replaced by another; average changes by a known amount; find the new/old value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Change in sum = n × change in average. One line.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Scores x in the nth innings and increases his average by d' — find new average or total runs.
pyqPatterns.approach: New total = (n−1)(A − d) + x = nA. Either form solves in one equation.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Boys/girls, workers/managers, two sections with separate averages and a combined average.
pyqPatterns.approach: Total sums, then divide. Or alligation: sizes are inversely proportional to distances from the combined average.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Average of first 10 naturals, 20 odd numbers, consecutive integers, squares.
pyqPatterns.approach: Formula table: (n+1)/2, n, n+1; consecutive → middle term.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Averages over overlapping windows of days/matches; one endpoint known; find the other.
pyqPatterns.approach: Subtract sums: the shared items cancel; difference of end items = window size × average difference.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Overall average plus averages of chunks, plus 'one number is k less/more than another'; find a specific term.
pyqPatterns.approach: Everything to sums, name the smallest unknown x, close the equation with the leftover total.

solvedExamples.q: The average of 8 numbers is 32.5. What is the sum of these numbers?
The average age of 20 boys is 12 years and that of 30 girls is 11 years. The average age of all the students is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: Weighted mean: the bigger group (girls) pulls the answer to 11.4 — closer to 11 than to 12.

solvedExamples.q: The average of 9 numbers is 27. If one number is excluded, the average of the remaining numbers becomes 25. The excluded number is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: Total sums both ways and subtract — no formula needed.

solvedExamples.q: The average of 8 numbers is 24. If the number 20 is replaced by 44, the new average will be:
solvedExamples.solution:
Increase in sum $= 44 - 20 = 24$.
Increase in average $= \frac{24}{8} = 3$ ⇒ new average $= 27$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Average jumps by (change in the number)/8 = 24/8 = 3 ⇒ 24 + 3 = 27.

solvedExamples.q: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings and thus increases his average by 3 runs. His average after the 17th innings is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the average after 17 innings be A.
Before: 16 innings at $(A - 3)$.
$16(A - 3) + 87 = 17A$ ⇒ $16A - 48 + 87 = 17A$ ⇒ $A = 39$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: New total = old total + 87: 17A = 16(A−3) + 87 ⇒ A = 39. (Quick check: old avg 36, total 576; 576 + 87 = 663 = 17 × 39 ✓)

practice.q: The average of the first 10 natural numbers is:
The average of 5 numbers is 27. If one more number 37 is included, the new average is:
practice.solution:
Old sum $= 135$. New sum $= 135 + 37 = 172$.
New average $= \frac{172}{6} = 28.5$.
practice.shortcut: 37 is 10 above the old average; the extra 10 spreads over 6 numbers: 27 + 10/6 = 28.5.

practice.q: The average of 6 numbers is 15. If each number is multiplied by 3 and then increased by 5, the new average is:
practice.shortcut: Linear operations pass through the average: ×3 then +5 ⇒ 50.

practice.q: The average of 5 consecutive numbers is 30. The largest of these numbers is:
practice.solution:
The middle (3rd) number is the average = 30.
Numbers: 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 ⇒ largest **32**.

practice.q: A batsman made 38.5 runs on average in 10 innings. His total runs are:
The average age of 30 students in a class is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average age increases by one year. The teacher's age is:
The average of 11 numbers is 50. The average of the first 6 numbers is 49 and that of the last 6 is 52. The 6th number is:
practice.shortcut: The 6th number is counted in both chunks: chunk sums add to total + 6th ⇒ 6th = 606 − 550 = 56.

practice.q: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings, which increases his average by 3 runs. His average after the 17th innings is:
The average marks of 60 students in a class is 50. The average marks of the 20 girls is 40. The average marks of the boys is:
practice.shortcut: Alligation too: 20 : 40 (girls : boys) splits the 40–55... the combined 50 sits 10 from girls' 40 and 5 from boys' 55 ⇒ sizes 2 : 1 ✓.

practice.q: The average monthly wage of 15 workers is ₹250. A manager is appointed and the average wage becomes ₹300. The manager's monthly wage is:
practice.shortcut: Manager = 300 + 15 × 50 = ₹1,050 (his own share plus the ₹50 raise for each of the 15).

practice.q: The average of the squares of the first 10 natural numbers is:
The average temperature of Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday is 37°C and of Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday is 34°C. If the temperature on Monday was 40°C, the temperature on Thursday is:

The average weight of three men A, B and C is 84 kg. A fourth man D joins them and the average weight of the four becomes 80 kg. If A weighs 78 kg and E replaces A, the average weight of B, C, D and E becomes 79 kg. E's weight is:
practice.shortcut: Build every sum stepwise: 252 → D = 68 → B + C = 174 → E = 316 − 242 = 74.

practice.q: The average of 8 numbers is 20. The average of the first two is 15.5 and that of the next three is $21\frac{1}{3}$. If the 6th number is 5 less than the 7th and the 8th is 7 more than the 7th, the 8th number is:
practice.solution:
Total = 160. First five total = 31 + 64 = 95.
Last three total = 65. Let the 6th be x: 6th + 7th + 8th = x + (x + 5) + (x + 12).
$3x + 17 = 65$ ⇒ $x = 16$ ⇒ 8th $= 16 + 12 = 28$.
practice.shortcut: Leftover sum 65 across three numbers whose mean is 65/3 — anchor on the 7th: 6th = 7th − 5, 8th = 7th + 7 ⇒ 7th = 21 ⇒ 8th = 28.

practice.q: The average age of a husband and wife at the time of their marriage was 23 years. After 5 years they have a one-year-old child. The average age of the family of three now is:
practice.solution:
Marriage total = 2 × 23 = 46. After 5 years: 46 + 5 + 5 = 56.
Child adds 1 year: total = 57.
Average $= \frac{57}{3} = 19$ years.
practice.shortcut: Both adults age 5 (total 56), child is 1 ⇒ 57/3 = 19. (Trap: forgetting to add the child's own age.)
